https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/71IColqD7xTAwKPAihMBamg5eo0=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x853:1281x854)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/04/a8/04a840a6-41bd-4f53-86c5-87ea8402f208/loren_elliott.jpg
blocks.c: a coyote walks on an elevated grassy area with San Francisco's skyline in the background

But by the start of the 2000s, the animals had mysteriously returned.
Afternoon Snack by Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/QbR38XBrBBynkM0AaQMMGq7JFcY=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(768x944:769x945)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/69/d5/69d5dcd3-723f-4782-a0e4-8d37989d7394/alexis_tinker-tsavalas.jpg
blocks.c: a close-up of two flies on a blade of grass, one predating on the other

blocks.x: The bubbles in the eyes of this unfortunate flesh fly—the victim in this predation event—suggest it has been injected with digestive enzymes from the larger robber fly, also known as an assassin fly. Those enzymes liquify the insect’s internal organs so that the robber fly can easily consume them.

In his portfolio spanning Germany and Northern Ireland, photographer Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas brings attention to tiny insects and arachnids. He created images with a large depth of field by stacking several photos that were focused in different areas.
Tiny Dancers by Kutub Uddin

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/8UM68pVTXhJgNy8vfXNR720BAzw=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x859:1281x860)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/dc/59/dc59e97e-951e-4247-a964-95f9d661a48f/kutub_uddin.jpg
blocks.c: orange stems grow from a log with fibrous threads on top of it, supporting green spheres with brown dots

blocks.x: Slime molds are mysterious and strange—not fitting into the categories of fungi, animals or plants, they can either be single cells or “supercells” with one cell membrane and many nuclei. Warning Sign by Francisco Negroni

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/Lry2o6l1y1rQN2yETFaW7MEtHfk=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x859:1281x860)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/01/ba/01badd30-ad12-4d1b-a9ab-bf021f3a804f/francisco_negroni.jpg
blocks.c: a dead puma is draped on top of a wire fence beside a field, its chin and tail resting on the wooden poles

blocks.x: In Argentina’s Santa Cruz province, where the hunting of pumas has been banned since last year, a dead puma is displayed tied to a fence as a hunting trophy. Photographer Francisco Negroni had “never witnessed or photographed” such a scene before, he says in a statement.

Humans who raise livestock might kill pumas to thwart livestock predation. According to the statement, keeping sheep indoors at night and using guard dogs could protect livestock without resorting to hunting the cats.
The Great Divide by Alex Visbal

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/cc5j05tshzWDi3yN_IQfBENTnkQ=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x853:1281x854)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/5d/ef/5def5b09-1f75-49a5-9667-019899eaf4bd/alex_visbal.jpg
blocks.c: an overhead view of the Great Salt Lake cut through by a manmade barrier. On the left the water is pink, and on the right it is more clear. Mountains rise in the background

blocks.x: A human-made line cuts through Stansbury Bay on Utah’s Great Salt Lake, cutting off an area turned pink by microbes that thrive in salty water.

Since this photo was taken, Utah has brought this area under conservation management, according to a statement.
Urban Jungle by Seth Forestson

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/eEIKb5_D65QaVjcZl6VCT73u72Y=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x902:1281x903)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/7a/fd/7afd5454-171f-420e-9c92-33afe6825a1a/seth_forestson.jpg
blocks.c: a monitor lizard carries a fish in an urban park with a city skyline in the background. A few others surround it, including a bird

blocks.x: The second-largest lizard species in the world, a common water monitor carries a fish in Bangkok. These animals spend most of the day warming their bodies in the sun, but they’re also generalist predators that will eat anything they can find—making them well-adapted for city living.
At Lumphini Park in Thailand, photographer Seth Forestson waited for the creatures to become active, then captured this shot—lying low against the mud to include the city skyline.
Making Morays by Tony Wu

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/fVDHwRhZyAtjNV_Fm4Cj8pnwyqI=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x859:1281x860)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/b3/e6/b3e6524e-7d40-4dcf-bd98-445b2a423075/tony_wu.jpg
blocks.c: a large moray eel and a much smaller one, illuminated by a point of light

blocks.x: The mating behavior of Abbott’s moray eels had long been a mystery. But a team of biologists and photographer Tony Wu have been working to shine light on this hidden activity for years.

With a red-light source and custom fisheye lens, Wu began photographing this male in 2024 in Kyushu, Japan. His resulting images, which are helping inform scientific studies, might be the first to document Abbott’s moray eel courtship and spawning.
Escape Artistry by Michał Michalski

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/SpK7oRMTT5OZDdeAVhV768ecWLI=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x859:1281x860)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/79/4b/794bec24-394a-4c5e-bdda-c37df11afc3e/micha_michalski.jpg
blocks.c: a flock of birds flies in front of leafless birch trees in dark lighting

blocks.x: This photograph might look like forest with crisp, autumn leaves, but don’t be deceived. Photographer Michał Michalski stood in front of a sunflower field in Poland, which was filled with feeding birds like goldfinches and bramblings. When a sparrowhawk startled the flock, the birds took off in unison, and Michalski captured their beating wings, blurred in front of the bare birch trees.
Shedding Light by Agorastos Papatsanis

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/80Y1zlKvSfXoA5qsgXulFcTx7po=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x859:1281x860)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/8f/1e/8f1ef0a7-bd9e-490a-a593-59c68ff98dd9/agorastos_papatsanis.jpg
blocks.c: the stalks of clumps of mushrooms glow yellow in the dark

blocks.x: Under ultraviolet light, the stems of these beautiful bonnet mushrooms glow in a bright yellow. Some fungi produce their own light, but these, captured by photographer Agorastos Papatsanis on the lower slopes of Greece’s Mount Olympus, work a little differently. They are fluorescent, meaning that they absorb light of one wavelength—ultraviolet—and re-emit it at another wavelength of visible light.
Night-Time Catch by Alex Lindbloom

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/gAWXeIR1JCXb_fT9i__zGLKL4Ys=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x963:1281x964)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/69/d4/69d43488-a5eb-4ed9-9cf5-27ec5aa0cca6/alex_lindbloom.jpg
blocks.c: an overhead view of a whale shark approaching a rectangular fishing platform in the dark

blocks.x: At dawn, this mobile net-fishing platform, or bagan, provided the only light for photographer Alex Lindbloom’s drone flying off the coast of Papua, Indonesia. He found a whale shark, the biggest fish species alive, curious about the fishers’ catch.

Whale sharks have declined by 50 percent globally over the past 75 years, and off West Papua, Indonesia, almost two-thirds of them have injuries from human-related causes, such as tour boats and fishing gear. Bagans might cause minor injuries, but they don’t typically result in death, per a statement, and local communities attract tourists with the predictable appearance of sharks at these platforms.
Scenes From the Swamp by Isak Pretorius

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/l8THg6tvsp6RZZlYATOnp_hRbbA=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x859:1281x860)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/bf/ec/bfec6dde-51a0-49ef-9464-3f62ac9adc8c/isak_pretorius.jpg
blocks.c: two large blue-gray birds with wide bills pull up vegetation, the rightmost bird spreading its wings

blocks.x: These flat-beaked shoebill birds might have been gathering nesting material as photographer Isak Pretorius watched them pull up vegetation and drop it. Shoebills are known to be elusive, so Pretorius felt lucky to find two of them when canoeing through Uganda’s Mabamba Swamp with a guide. Classified as a vulnerable species, fewer than 5,300 adult shoebills are thought to remain in the wild.
A Watchful Eye by Aaron Sanders

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/_jIc3RDLhpaesF70Vhaj5nHgxqU=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x859:1281x860)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/c3/e6/c3e6df39-ff5c-4f1d-8ead-46fac9a6b492/aaron_sanders.jpg
blocks.c: an octopus is hidden behind a piece of kelp with only one eye showing in the light and its suckers slightly visible through the kelp

blocks.x: A common octopus makes eye contact with photographer Aaron Sanders from behind a curtain of kelp. “We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity,” he says in a statement. The silhouette of the cephalopod’s suckers can be seen through the seaweed.

Sanders spotted the creature when diving off England’s Porthkerris Beach. Common octopuses have been spotted more frequently in the region during the past two years. They prefer warm waters, typically found around the Mediterranean, but this recent “bloom” in abundance is thought to be linked to rising sea temperatures.
The Meeting Place by James Lewin

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/Jh7OufnuV7IZ7dhRsh8Nav1qDnI=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x658:1281x659)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/54/24/54244a11-031f-43a2-a32b-2ad601ce2fc4/james_lewin.jpg
blocks.c: an elephant, several giraffes and a handful of zebras gather at a watering hole, with the elephant spraying a zebra's head with water from its trunk

blocks.x: Giraffes, zebras and elephants gather at a watering hole for a drink in Kenya’s Chyulu Hills National Park. Herbivores might spend more time in these areas when elephants are around, potentially because their large size could deter predators. Here, a young male elephant sprays zebras in a scene captured by photographer James Lewin.
Shifting Sand by Sitaram Raul

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/JZOQ7UWdEE2CvzHXIFAV_Zlu_sI=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x859:1281x860)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/69/ec/69ece6fe-54f4-4b01-a478-bb09adf8b6e4/sitaram_raul.jpg
blocks.c: a scorpion burrows into the sand, tossing grains of sand behind it, only its rear legs and curled tail visible

blocks.x: A scorpion tosses sand as it burrows to escape the heat of the rising sun in India’s Thar Desert. Photographer Sitaram Raul timed the shot to get the sand grains suspended in the air. Buthacus scorpions like this one use stiff bristles as snowshoes to keep from sinking into the dunes.
“What you see in the final image is just a small part of the story,” Raul writes on Instagram. “Behind it are hours in the field, patience, curiosity and a desire to see nature a little differently.”
Flight of the Bumblebee by Amelie Davis

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/65qdZlPiqpLiuq8FdVX5iYcZbHE=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x963:1281x964)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/31/4b/314b66da-579f-481b-8c06-0fa806164ace/amelie_davis.jpg
blocks.c: a bumblebee flies in a garden moving toward the camera in bright light

blocks.x: Using her dad’s iPhone, young photographer Amelie Davis captured a common carder bee mid-flight in a garden in southern England. Davis had spent months photographing bees, but on this particular day, the flowers were “teeming with bees,” she says in a statement.
Birdsong Painted in Light by Konrad Gräeter

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/g4Ht3ALwS4Qux__faufPw5X_OYc=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1280x853:1281x854)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/5c/aa/5caad624-036b-40f5-898e-082dc913c20c/konrad_graeter.jpg
blocks.c: a blackbird sings from a sparse branch in near-darkness

blocks.x: Male Eurasian blackbirds sit on elevated perches and sing to attract mates in spring—and their most complex songs come in the morning, according to a statement. Females, in reply, give a softer tune.

In a German vineyard, young photographer Konrad Gräeter captured an image of this male blackbird singing, framed through the foliage at dawn. “With this image I try to show that the beauty of nature is all around us, if we only look,” Gräeter writes on Instagram.

When a sparrowhawk startled the flock, the birds took off in unison, and Michalski captured their beating wings, blurred in front of the bare birch trees.

Shedding Light by Agorastos Papatsanis

Under ultraviolet light, the stems of these beautiful bonnet mushrooms glow in a bright yellow. Some fungi produce their own light, but these, captured by photographer Agorastos Papatsanis on the lower slopes of Greece’s Mount Olympus, work a little differently. They are fluorescent, meaning that they absorb light of one wavelength—ultraviolet—and re-emit it at another wavelength of visible light.

Night-Time Catch by Alex Lindbloom

At dawn, this mobile net-fishing platform, or bagan, provided the only light for photographer Alex Lindbloom’s drone flying off the coast of Papua, Indonesia. He found a whale shark, the biggest fish species alive, curious about the fishers’ catch.

Whale sharks have declined by 50 percent globally over the past 75 years, and off West Papua, Indonesia, almost two-thirds of them have injuries from human-related causes, such as tour boats and fishing gear. Bagans might cause minor injuries, but they don’t typically result in death, per a statement, and local communities attract tourists with the predictable appearance of sharks at these platforms.

Scenes From the Swamp by Isak Pretorius

These flat-beaked shoebill birds might have been gathering nesting material as photographer Isak Pretorius watched them pull up vegetation and drop it. Shoebills are known to be elusive, so Pretorius felt lucky to find two of them when canoeing through Uganda’s Mabamba Swamp with a guide. Classified as a vulnerable species, fewer than 5,300 adult shoebills are thought to remain in the wild.

A Watchful Eye by Aaron Sanders

A common octopus makes eye contact with photographer Aaron Sanders from behind a curtain of kelp. “We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity,” he says in a statement. The silhouette of the cephalopod’s suckers can be seen through the seaweed.

Sanders spotted the creature when diving off England’s Porthkerris Beach. Common octopuses have been spotted more frequently in the region during the past two years. They prefer warm waters, typically found around the Mediterranean, but this recent “bloom” in abundance is thought to be linked to rising sea temperatures.

The Meeting Place by James Lewin

Giraffes, zebras and elephants gather at a watering hole for a drink in Kenya’s Chyulu Hills National Park. Herbivores might spend more time in these areas when elephants are around, potentially because their large size could deter predators. Here, a young male elephant sprays zebras in a scene captured by photographer James Lewin.

Shifting Sand by Sitaram Raul

A scorpion tosses sand as it burrows to escape the heat of the rising sun in India’s Thar Desert. Photographer Sitaram Raul timed the shot to get the sand grains suspended in the air. Buthacus scorpions like this one use stiff bristles as snowshoes to keep from sinking into the dunes.

“What you see in the final image is just a small part of the story,” Raul writes on Instagram. “Behind it are hours in the field, patience, curiosity and a desire to see nature a little differently.”

Flight of the Bumblebee by Amelie Davis

Using her dad’s iPhone, young photographer Amelie Davis captured a common carder bee mid-flight in a garden in southern England. Davis had spent months photographing bees, but on this particular day, the flowers were “teeming with bees,” she says in a statement.

Birdsong Painted in Light by Konrad Gräeter

Male Eurasian blackbirds sit on elevated perches and sing to attract mates in spring—and their most complex songs come in the morning, according to a statement. Females, in reply, give a softer tune.

In a German vineyard, young photographer Konrad Gräeter captured an image of this male blackbird singing, framed through the foliage at dawn. “With this image I try to show that the beauty of nature is all around us, if we only look,” Gräeter writes on Instagram.
